app/models/blocked_email.rb:15 — The read-modify-save increment loses hits when concurrent checks read the same match_count and save the same incremented value; use an atomic database increment.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:17 — Match statistics updates join the user save transaction and roll back when blocked-email validation rejects registration, leaving match_count and last_match_at unchanged.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: in BlockedEmail.should_block?, the method calls record.save to update match_count and last_match_at. This is called from EmailValidator.validate_each during User model validation. If the email is blocked, an error is added to the record, which will cause the User save transaction to fail and roll back. Since the BlockedEmail.save happens within the same request/validation context, if the User creation is wrapped in a transaction (which ActiveRecord does by default), the BlockedEmail statistics update would be rolled back along with it. The diff shows this flow: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block? which saves statistics, then adds an error, causing the User save to fail.
